name: Hiroshima & Miyajima
tagline: A red torii gate on the sea and a city of peace
intro: This route spends one day at each of the two World Heritage sites (the Atomic Bomb Dome and Itsukushima Shrine), then uses any spare days to branch out to the hillside lanes of Onomichi, the Yamato Museum in Kure, or the old streets of Takehara. Okonomiyaki, oysters and conger eel rice bowls are cheap and filling, so it works well for family trips and first-time visitors to Japan. You can get around the city by streetcar and the surrounding area by JR, so a rental car is not needed.
season_notes: Spring: cherry blossoms at Peace Memorial Park and Miyajima (early April), with the best weather / Summer: hot and humid, and lodging is pricey during the week of the August 6 Peace Memorial Ceremony / Autumn: autumn leaves at Miyajima's Momijidani (mid to late November), and oyster season begins / Winter: snow is rare, oysters taste their best, and fewer tourists make it quiet
airport_access/0/note: Departs to match flight arrivals, every 20 to 30 minutes. Fare ¥1,400~1,500 (to be confirmed). Road conditions can add about 10 minutes
airport_access/1/note: Take the bus to JR Shiraichi Station (15 min, ¥490, to be confirmed), then the Sanyo Main Line for 45 min. The limousine bus is easier if you have a lot of luggage
getting_around: In the city, the Hiroden streetcar (flat fare of ¥240 within the city zone, to be confirmed) takes you to Peace Memorial Park, Hondori and Hiroshima Castle. Since summer 2025, streetcars run straight into the second floor of the Hiroshima Station building, which makes transfers easier. To Miyajima, take the JR Sanyo Main Line to Miyajimaguchi (28 min), then the ferry (10 min). Onomichi, Kure and Takehara are easy day trips by JR or express bus, and Google Maps directions work accurately.
transport_pass: The Hiroden streetcar and ferry 1-day pass (all streetcar lines plus the Miyajima ferry, around ¥1,000, to be confirmed) is the better deal on your Miyajima day. If you ride the streetcar 3 or more times in a day, the streetcar 1-day pass (around ¥700, to be confirmed) also pays for itself. For JR sections, simply tapping an IC card (Suica or ICOCA) is the easiest way.
spots/0/desc: An airport on a hilltop, 50 km east of downtown Hiroshima. There are direct flights from Incheon, and the limousine bus is the easiest way into the city.
spots/0/access: About 50 min by limousine bus to the Shinkansen exit of Hiroshima Station
spots/0/tip: For your flight home, taking a bus 2 hours before departure leaves a comfortable margin. The duty-free shop is small, so it is better to buy souvenirs at Ekie in Hiroshima Station
spots/0/kid_tip: You can watch planes take off and land from the observation deck on the 2nd floor
spots/1/desc: The starting point of your trip, where the Shinkansen, JR, streetcars and buses all meet. The station building Minamoa, which opened in spring 2025, and Ekie are packed with okonomiyaki restaurants and souvenir shops.
spots/1/access: Last stop of the airport limousine bus
spots/1/tip: Board the streetcar from the platform on the 2nd floor of the station building. Most coin lockers are near the Shinkansen exit
spots/1/kid_tip: Many restaurants in the 2nd-floor dining area of Ekie have high chairs for children
spots/2/desc: An express bus terminal on the 3rd floor of the Sogo department store. The Kaguyahime bus to Takehara and the airport limousine buses leave from here. It is a 5-minute walk from Peace Memorial Park, so it is handy for catching a bus right after sightseeing in the city.
spots/2/tip: Airport buses also leave from here, so if you stay in the city center on your last day, you do not need to go back to the station
spots/3/desc: A large park built near the center of the atomic bombing, with the Cenotaph for the Atomic Bomb Victims, the Children's Peace Monument and the Flame of Peace lined up in a row. A promenade continues across the river to the Atomic Bomb Dome.
spots/3/access: 3-minute walk from Genbaku Dome-mae streetcar stop
spots/3/tip: Early morning or around sunset has fewer people and better photos. Around August 6 it is extremely crowded because of ceremonies
spots/3/kid_tip: The paper crane display in front of the Children's Peace Monument is a good way to explain things to children
spots/4/desc: The skeletal remains of the former Industrial Promotion Hall, which stood right next to the hypocenter in 1945, now a World Heritage site. You can see it from any angle along the riverside promenade, and it is lit up at night.
spots/4/access: Right in front of Genbaku Dome-mae streetcar stop
spots/4/tip: The view looking down from the observation deck of the Orizuru Tower across the way is a different angle
spots/5/desc: A museum exhibiting belongings and photographs from the time of the bombing. The content is heavy, but it is a must-visit if you come to Hiroshima. Korean audio guides and explanatory texts are available.
spots/5/access: South end of Peace Memorial Park
spots/5/hours: Mar to Jul and Sep to Nov 7:30–18:00, Aug 7:30–19:00, Dec to Feb 8:30–17:00 (last entry 30 min before closing)
spots/5/closed: Dec 30–31, and a few days of equipment maintenance in mid-February (to be confirmed)
spots/5/tip: Group visits are heavy after 10 a.m., so right after opening or after 4 p.m. is quieter. Booking online can shorten the wait
spots/5/kid_tip: Some exhibits are intense for lower elementary school children, so it is better to keep it short and focus on the East Building
spots/6/desc: A wooden-deck observation platform on the roof of the building right next to the Atomic Bomb Dome, with a sweeping view of Peace Memorial Park and the city. You can fold a paper crane and drop it down a wall of cranes.
spots/6/access: 1-minute walk from Genbaku Dome-mae streetcar stop
spots/6/tip: The admission fee is on the high side, so it is worth it on a clear day around sunset. The 1st-floor gift shop and cafe are free to enter
spots/6/kid_tip: Kids love the spiral slide that comes down from the roof (next to Orizuru Square)
spots/7/desc: A castle on flat ground built by Mori Terumoto, with a moat and a reconstructed main keep in the middle of the city. The main keep closed on March 22, 2026 because of aging and earthquake-resistance issues, so for now it can only be seen from outside, but the Ninomaru (reconstructed gate and turrets) and a walk around the moat are still possible.
spots/7/access: 12-minute walk from Kamiyacho-higashi streetcar stop, 10-minute walk from Prefectural Office-mae Station on the Astram Line
spots/7/hours: Grounds always open (Ninomaru 9:00–17:30, to be confirmed)
spots/7/closed: Main keep interior closed from 2026-03-22 (long term)
spots/7/tip: The main keep exhibits are moving to the Sannomaru History Museum, due to open in 2027. An efficient route is to walk once around the moat, take photos, and head on to Shukkeien
spots/7/kid_tip: It is a nice walk watching the carp and turtles in the moat
spots/8/desc: A strolling garden created in 1620 by the lord of Hiroshima, with an arched bridge and tea house in the middle of its pond. It is a 15-minute walk from Hiroshima Castle and especially beautiful during cherry blossom and autumn leaf seasons.
spots/8/tip: A combo ticket with the neighboring Prefectural Art Museum is available. Walking with an umbrella on a rainy day is also atmospheric
spots/8/kid_tip: Children can feed the carp (for a fee), so they do not get bored
spots/9/desc: A covered arcade shopping street that begins east of Peace Memorial Park, lined with drugstores, general stores, cafes and okonomiyaki restaurants. It is pleasant to walk even in the rain, and in the evening it connects to the Nagarekawa nightlife district in the next lane.
spots/9/access: Right in front of Hondori streetcar stop
spots/9/tip: Hiroshima Andersen's flagship bakery and Don Quijote are along the way. Exchanging money is better at the banks here than at the station
spots/9/kid_tip: It is an arcade, so it is easy to get around with a stroller
spots/10/desc: A famous food building in Hiroshima, with about 20 okonomiyaki shops lined up like food stalls on floors 2 to 4. Each shop has a slightly different taste and atmosphere, so you rarely go wrong by choosing one with a short line.
spots/10/tip: The basic version with soba (soba niku tama) is around ¥1,000. Seats are counters in front of the griddle, so with children choose a shop with tables further inside
spots/10/kid_tip: The griddle is hot, so seat young children on the inner side, next to a parent
spots/11/desc: An automobile museum inside Mazda's headquarters, where you tour the Le Mans-winning car, rotary engines and the assembly plant line. It is free, but advance reservations on the official website are required, and it is open on weekdays only.
spots/11/access: Shuttle from a 5-minute walk from JR Mukainada Station, or 5 minutes by JR from Hiroshima Station
spots/11/hours: Reserved time slots (weekday mornings and afternoons, to be confirmed)
spots/11/tip: Slots fill up about a month ahead, so book as soon as your schedule is set. Whether Korean-language tours are offered is to be confirmed
spots/11/kid_tip: Elementary school children especially enjoy the section where you watch the actual production line
spots/12/desc: A ferry pier just a 5-minute walk from JR Miyajimaguchi Station, where two companies, JR and Matsudai, run ferries to the island every 10 to 15 minutes. Inside the terminal are conger eel rice bowl shops and souvenir stores.
spots/12/access: 28 min from Hiroshima Station on the JR Sanyo Main Line, 70 min by streetcar
spots/12/tip: The JR ferry takes a route that passes close to the torii gate between about 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. Since 2023, a ¥100 Miyajima visitor tax has been added to the boarding ticket
spots/12/kid_tip: If you go out on deck, the torii gate is visible the whole 10 minutes, and kids love it
spots/13/desc: A shrine with corridors built over the sea. At low tide you can walk right up to the great torii gate, and at high tide the whole shrine looks like it is floating on the water. It is a World Heritage site and one of the Three Views of Japan.
spots/13/hours: 6:30–18:00 (17:00–18:30 depending on the season, to be confirmed)
spots/13/tip: Check the high and low tide times for the day in advance and plan your schedule to see both scenes. Admission ¥300 (combo ticket with the Treasure Hall ¥500, to be confirmed)
spots/13/kid_tip: Deer will eat paper and maps, so be careful with anything in your hands. At low tide there are many small crabs on the tidal flat
spots/14/desc: A 350 m shopping street running from the ferry pier to the shrine, packed with grilled oysters, momiji manju and conger eel rice bowl shops. The world's largest rice paddle (shakushi) is on display.
spots/14/tip: Most shops close around 5 p.m., so eat during the day. If you stay on the island, you get the quiet streets at night all to yourself
spots/14/kid_tip: You can watch the machines baking momiji manju through the glass window
spots/15/desc: A huge wooden hall that Toyotomi Hideyoshi left unfinished. It has no walls, so the wind blows through and you can look down at the sea. Together with the red five-story pagoda beside it, it is a good spot for photographing the whole shrine.
spots/15/access: On the hill above the entrance to Itsukushima Shrine
spots/15/tip: You can sit and rest on the wooden floor, so it is also a good place to escape the summer heat
spots/16/desc: The oldest Shingon Buddhist temple on Miyajima, famous for its 500 rakan statues and the prayer wheels along the stair railings. Tourists crowd the shrine, so this place is relatively quiet.
spots/16/access: 10-minute walk from the exit of Itsukushima Shrine
spots/16/tip: The grounds are prettiest during the autumn leaves in mid-November. It is also the entrance to the Mount Misen hiking trail (Daishoin course)
spots/16/kid_tip: Playing a game of finding the rakan statues, each with a different expression, keeps children from getting bored
spots/17/desc: From Momijidani Park, you transfer between two gondolas up to Shishiiwa Observation Deck, partway up Mount Misen. The islands of the Seto Inland Sea spread out below, and the summit is another 30 minutes on foot.
spots/17/access: 25-minute walk from the ferry pier, or the free shuttle bus (to the entrance of Momijidani Park)
spots/17/hours: Around 9:00–16:00 (varies by season, to be confirmed)
spots/17/closed: Closed twice a year for regular maintenance (to be confirmed)
spots/17/tip: Round trip ¥2,000. Lines get long after 2 p.m., so go up in the morning. If you plan to go to the summit, sneakers are a must
spots/17/kid_tip: Going only as far as Shishiiwa Observation Deck is still well worth it, and strollers can only go as far as the shuttle bus
spots/18/desc: At 535 m above sea level, the highest peak on Miyajima, with a 360-degree view of the Seto Inland Sea from an observation deck on a huge granite rock. You also pass Reikado Hall, which has a flame said to have burned for 1,200 years.
spots/18/access: 30-minute walk (uphill) from Shishiiwa Station on the ropeway
spots/18/tip: Be sure to check the last descending ropeway time and start down an hour early. Bring drinks with you in advance
spots/18/kid_tip: Upper elementary school children and older can manage the walk; for younger ones, stop at Shishiiwa Observation Deck
spots/19/desc: A small station standing right by the sea, rebuilt in 2019, with a 2nd-floor observation deck overlooking the Onomichi Channel. Inside the station building are an Onomichi ramen shop and a cafe.
spots/19/access: About 1 hr 25 min from Hiroshima Station on the JR Sanyo Main Line; by Shinkansen, go to Shin-Onomichi Station (15 min by bus)
spots/19/tip: There are few coin lockers, so leave big luggage in Hiroshima. Get a map of the hillside lanes at the tourist information center in front of the station
spots/20/desc: A hilltop park reached in 3 minutes by ropeway. From PEAK, the observation deck built in 2022, you can see the Onomichi Channel and the islands of the Shimanami Kaido in one sweep. It is a cherry blossom spot in spring.
spots/20/access: Right in front of the Senkojisan Ropeway summit station (one way ¥500, round trip ¥700, 9:00–17:15)
spots/20/tip: The classic way is to take the ropeway up and walk down via the Literary Path and Senkoji Temple
spots/20/kid_tip: There is a small playground and lawn next to the observation deck, which makes it a good place to rest
spots/21/desc: A temple built clinging to a cliff and founded in 806, where you look down at the sea from the veranda of the red main hall. You will naturally stop by on the way down from the park.
spots/21/tip: It is fun to read the legend of the Jewel Rock (Tama no Iwa) beside the main hall before you go. There are bell-ringing times (such as noon)
spots/21/kid_tip: There are many stairs, so you will have to leave the stroller behind
spots/22/desc: In the narrow alleys below Senkoji, painted stone cats (Fukuishi Neko) are hidden, and there are plenty of real stray cats too. Small cafes and galleries made from renovated abandoned houses line the way.
spots/22/tip: The paths are narrow and slippery, so be careful after rain. Do not feed the cats
spots/22/kid_tip: Walk while counting how many stone cats you can find
spots/23/desc: An old shopping street that stretches 1.2 km east from the station, with a mix of Showa-era signs, bookshops, general stores and ramen shops. It has also often been used as a movie location.
spots/23/hours: Varies by shop (many shops closed on Tuesdays)
spots/23/tip: Onomichi U2 (a complex converted from a warehouse) is on the waterfront west of the station, in the opposite direction from the shopping street
spots/24/name: Takehara Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings
spots/24/desc: A merchant town that grew rich on salt and sake in the Edo period remains intact and is called the 'Little Kyoto of Aki.' The birthplace of Taketsuru Masataka, founder of Nikka Whisky (Taketsuru Sake Brewery), and old houses line a stretch of 300 m.
spots/24/access: About 1 hr 20 min by Kaguyahime express bus from Hiroshima Bus Center (¥1,300, to be confirmed), or a 15-minute walk from JR Takehara Station
spots/24/closed: Many open-to-the-public houses are closed on Tuesdays (to be confirmed)
spots/24/tip: The signature photo is looking down at the tiled roofs from Saihoji Temple's Fumeikaku (temple pavilion) on the hill. At the end of October, bamboo lanterns are lit at night during the 'Takehara Bamboo Festival'
spots/24/kid_tip: The roads are flat and good for walking with children, and there is a park near Takehara Station
spots/25/desc: A small island 15 minutes by boat from Tadanoumi Port, home to several hundred wild rabbits. The ruins of a former poison gas factory remain, so you can combine peace education with a nature experience.
spots/25/access: 15-minute ferry after a 7-minute walk from JR Tadanoumi Station (one way ¥360, to be confirmed)
spots/25/tip: No rabbit food is sold on the island, so buy rabbit food (vegetables) at Tadanoumi Port. Walking around the island takes 1 hour, and bicycles can be rented in front of the resort lodging
spots/25/kid_tip: The rabbits are used to people, so it is a good place for kids to feed them, but do not pick them up
spots/26/desc: The central station of a former naval port city, reached in 32 minutes from Hiroshima on the JR Kure Line rapid service. The Yamato Museum is a 5-minute walk from the station over a pedestrian bridge.
spots/26/access: About 32 min from Hiroshima Station on the JR Kure Line rapid Akiji Liner (¥510, to be confirmed)
spots/26/tip: If you take the pedestrian bridge on the Yumetown side inside the station, it leads to the museum with no traffic lights
spots/27/desc: A maritime museum that tells the history of the Kure shipyard, where the battleship Yamato was built, through a 1/10-scale Yamato model and real fighter plane engines. It reopened on April 23, 2026 after renovations lasting over a year.
spots/27/closed: Tuesdays (next weekday if a holiday), New Year holidays (to be confirmed)
spots/27/tip: After the renovation, the admission fee rose to ¥1,000. Combine it with the neighboring Tetsu no Kujira-kan (free) for half a day
spots/27/kid_tip: The 3rd-floor science experience corner has a ship-steering simulator where kids play for a long time
spots/28/desc: A Maritime Self-Defense Force museum with the retired submarine Akishio placed whole on land, where you can go inside to the control room and the bunks. Admission is free.
spots/28/access: Right next to the Yamato Museum
spots/28/closed: Tuesdays (next weekday if a holiday), Dec 29–Jan 3
spots/28/tip: The passages inside the submarine are narrow, so leave big backpacks in a locker. The 1st-floor cafe serves navy curry
spots/28/kid_tip: You can turn the periscope yourself, and it is the place kids like best
spots/29/desc: A seaside park where you can see Maritime Self-Defense Force submarines and escort ships moored right in front of you. On Sunday mornings, escort ship open-house events are sometimes held.
spots/29/access: 10 min by bus or 25-minute walk from Kure Station
spots/29/tip: Take a walk together with the red brick warehouse street. A naval port cruise from Kure Port (30 min, around ¥1,500, to be confirmed) gets you even closer
restaurants/0/desc: A shop founded in 1950 and called the originator of Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki. It has table seats, so many families come, and while the line is long, turnover is quick.
restaurants/0/hours: 11:30–14:30, 17:30–21:00 (Sat, Sun and holidays from 11:00 and 17:00, to be confirmed)
restaurants/0/tips/0: Arrive before the lunch opening to get the first seating
restaurants/0/tips/1: There are also branches at Ekie and the Shinkansen exit
restaurants/1/signature: Soba niku tama (with extra green onion)
restaurants/1/desc: An okonomiyaki restaurant that locals name first, known for crispy noodles and soft-cooked eggs. It opens only in the evening and the line is long, so the trick is to go before opening.
restaurants/1/hours: 16:00–22:30 (Sun and holidays until 21:00, to be confirmed)
restaurants/1/closed: Mondays, and the 1st and 3rd Tuesdays (to be confirmed)
restaurants/1/tips/1: Mostly counter seats, so it is somewhat inconvenient for young children
restaurants/2/desc: A shop 2 minutes on foot from the Atomic Bomb Dome, used to foreign guests, with English and Korean menus. It is the most convenient spot to stop by before or after visiting Peace Memorial Park.
restaurants/2/closed: Tuesdays, and the 2nd and 4th Wednesdays (to be confirmed)
restaurants/2/tips/0: The lunchtime line is long, so go at 11:00 or after 14:00
restaurants/3/desc: A long-established shop with the longest line on the 2nd-floor okonomiyaki street in Ekie at Hiroshima Station. It is a good place to stop by with your luggage right after arriving or just before leaving.
restaurants/3/tips/0: If the line is long, the other shops on the same floor are of similar quality
restaurants/4/signature: Oyster kaiseki course, lunchtime oyster set meal
restaurants/4/desc: An oyster specialty restaurant on a boat floating on the river in front of Peace Memorial Park, the most famous oyster restaurant in Hiroshima. The lunch set meal is in the ¥3,000 range, so it is easier on the budget.
restaurants/4/tips/1: Farmed oysters mean you can eat them even in summer
restaurants/5/desc: A leading shop for Hiroshima-style tsukemen, where cold noodles are dipped in a spicy soy-based sauce. It comes piled with cabbage and boiled egg, making a light meal.
restaurants/5/tips/0: Spice levels 1 to 2 are fine for most Korean palates
restaurants/5/tips/1: There is also a branch at Ekie in Hiroshima Station
restaurants/6/name: Musubi no Musashi Shinkansen Exit Branch
restaurants/6/desc: A rice ball specialty shop known as the picnic lunch of Hiroshima locals. It is a good place to buy a bento to eat on the morning train to Miyajima or Onomichi.
restaurants/6/tips/0: Opens early, so it works for train bento
restaurants/7/desc: A bakery reopened in 2020 in a building that survived the atomic bombing, with a bakery and cafe on the 1st floor and a buffet restaurant on the 2nd. It is a good spot for coffee and a snack during a stroll along Hondori.
restaurants/7/tips/0: Good for buying bread for breakfast
restaurants/7/tips/1: Reservations are recommended for the 2nd-floor buffet
restaurants/8/desc: The originator of the conger eel rice bowl, founded in 1901 and located in front of Miyajimaguchi Station. The restaurant has a long line, but you can buy a bento relatively quickly and eat it on the ferry or on the island.
restaurants/8/hours: Restaurant 10:00–19:00, bento from 9:00 (Wednesdays bento only, to be confirmed)
restaurants/8/tips/0: Waits of over an hour are normal at the restaurant
restaurants/8/tips/1: The bento is made to taste good even when cold
restaurants/9/signature: Grilled oysters, oyster set meal (Kakiya teishoku)
restaurants/9/desc: An oyster specialty restaurant right in the middle of Omotesando shopping street, serving charcoal-grilled oysters, fried oysters and oyster rice as a set meal. The interior has clean white walls, so many women and families come.
restaurants/9/hours: 10:00–18:00 (closes when ingredients run out, to be confirmed)
restaurants/9/tips/0: The line is long at the lunch peak (12:00 to 13:00)
restaurants/9/tips/1: You can also just buy grilled oysters at the front of the shop and eat them there
restaurants/10/signature: Momiji manju (red bean, custard, cheese), momiji manju making experience
restaurants/10/desc: A momiji manju shop founded in 1932 that sells maple-leaf-shaped cakes fresh from the oven. You can bake them yourself in the workshop, so it is a nice stop with children.
restaurants/10/tips/0: The neighboring shop Koyama is also famous for fried momiji manju (age momiji)
restaurants/11/desc: A cafe that roasts its own beans inside Omotesando shopping street, where you can rest by a 2nd-floor window looking down on the street. It is a good place to rest your legs while strolling the shopping street.
restaurants/11/tips/0: After 3 p.m. there are more open seats
restaurants/11/tips/1: The coffee beans make a good gift
restaurants/12/name: Onomichi Ramen Tani Station Building Branch
restaurants/12/signature: Onomichi ramen (soy sauce broth, pork back fat)
restaurants/12/desc: An Onomichi ramen shop inside the Onomichi Station building, so you can eat as soon as you arrive. Typical of the Onomichi style, it has a small-fish broth topped with pork back fat, and the portion is just right.
restaurants/12/tips/0: It has 23 counter seats, so turnover is quick
restaurants/12/tips/1: 15 minutes before your train is enough
restaurants/13/desc: A popular ramen shop near the east end of the shopping street, whose signature dish is ramen topped with big pieces of braised pork belly. It has table seats, so many families come.
restaurants/13/tips/0: The lunch peak wait is around 30 minutes
restaurants/13/tips/1: Stop by while you walk to the end of the shopping street
restaurants/14/signature: Lemon cake, Setouchi lemon drink, Bertie bakery bread
restaurants/14/desc: A cafe inside Onomichi U2, a complex converted from an old seaside warehouse, with a mix of cycling travelers and families. It is a nice place to rest on the waterfront terrace watching the islands and boats.
restaurants/14/tips/0: The restaurant 'The Restaurant' in the same building serves a dinner course
restaurants/14/tips/1: 5 minutes from Onomichi Station toward the waterfront
restaurants/15/signature: Takehara-yaki (batter with sake lees and vinegar)
restaurants/15/desc: An okonomiyaki shop that uses an old house in the preservation district as it is, which became known when the TV drama 'Massan' was filmed here. It serves a local style with sake lees from a Takehara sake brewery mixed into the batter.
restaurants/15/tips/0: There are few restaurants on the old street, so stop by early for lunch
restaurants/15/tips/1: It has floor seating, which is comfortable with children
restaurants/16/signature: Kure cold noodles (flat noodles, tangy soy broth)
restaurants/16/desc: The originator of Kure's famous cold noodles, a shop that has kept going for over 60 years. Unlike Korean naengmyeon, chilled Chinese-style noodles are served in a sweet and sour soy broth, so children eat it well too.
restaurants/16/hours: Around 11:30–15:00 (closes when ingredients run out, to be confirmed)
restaurants/16/tips/0: It is open for lunch only and the line is long, so arrive around 11:00
restaurants/16/tips/1: The regular noodle portion is enough for women
restaurants/17/signature: Submarine curry (official Maritime Self-Defense Force recipe)
restaurants/17/desc: A restaurant on the 2nd floor of the building next to the Yamato Museum, known for its navy curry that recreates the curry recipes of Maritime Self-Defense Force ships. It follows naturally as lunch after visiting the museum.
restaurants/17/tips/0: The menu explaining Friday curry culture is interesting
restaurants/17/tips/1: You can see the harbor from the window seats
restaurants/18/signature: Fried cake (fried red bean doughnut, around ¥100 each)
restaurants/18/desc: A fried red bean bun sold in the Kure shopping street since 1947, known for its crispy outside and moist bean filling. It is nice to buy one or two as a snack on the walk from Kure Station.
restaurants/18/hours: 10:00–18:00 (closes when sold out, to be confirmed)
restaurants/18/tips/0: It tastes best eaten right away, fresh from the fryer
hotels/0/desc: A JR-group hotel attached directly to the Shinkansen exit of Hiroshima Station, so you can start every day trip to Miyajima, Onomichi and Kure from the station. The rooms are not large but are clean, and the breakfast buffet is excellent.
hotels/0/pts/0: Directly connected to the station, so it is the easiest for trips to nearby areas
hotels/0/pts/1: Right in front of the airport limousine bus stop
hotels/0/pts/2: Connected underground to the Ekie dining area and gift shops
hotels/1/desc: A hotel with a large public bath between Hondori shopping street and Peace Memorial Park, with free late-night ramen and a sauna. The rooms were refreshed in spring 2026 (to be confirmed).
hotels/1/pts/0: The large bath and sauna are great for relieving a day's fatigue
hotels/1/pts/2: Free late-night ramen and a good breakfast
hotels/2/desc: A high-rise hotel connected by a pedestrian bridge to the Shinkansen exit of Hiroshima Station, with large rooms, a pool and a spa. It suits family trips and anniversary trips.
hotels/2/pts/0: Large rooms and views from the upper floors
hotels/2/pts/2: Directly connected to the station, so no moving around with luggage
hotels/3/desc: A long-established ryokan inside Momijidani Park, founded in 1854, known for its stream-side detached rooms, hot spring public bath and Seto Inland Sea kaiseki. It is the leading place to stay for enjoying Miyajima at night after the day-trippers leave.
hotels/3/pts/0: See the Momijidani autumn leaves and stream from your room
hotels/3/pts/1: Hot spring public bath and carefully prepared kaiseki
hotels/3/pts/2: Free pickup and drop-off at the ferry pier (contact in advance)

variants/2/title: Rainy Day Plan (focused on indoor museums)
variants/2/theme: A 2-night, 3-day trip with less time under an umbrella
variants/2/summary: Fill the first day with covered places such as the museum, Orizuru Tower and the arcade shopping street, and spend the second day at two museums in Kure and shopping in the station building. On the last day, if the rain stops, spend half a day on Miyajima; if it keeps raining, switch to Shukkeien and Hondori.

bplan/0/desc: When the Kure museums are closed on Tuesday or it rains, fill half a day at this free, reservation-only automobile museum (weekdays only).
bplan/1/desc: An art museum next to Shukkeien with a combo ticket. On a rainy day, you can spend an hour indoors instead of strolling the garden.
bplan/2/desc: With children, go on your Takehara day, 15 minutes by boat from Tadanoumi Port. Feeding the rabbits makes half a day fly by.
bplan/3/desc: A small aquarium on the way to Daishoin, good when it rains or children get bored at the shrine. It has Seto Inland Sea fish and otters.
bplan/4/desc: If you have time left in Onomichi, rent a bicycle at U2, cross by boat to Mukaishima and ride along the coast for 1 to 2 hours.
bplan/5/desc: If you have a rental car or time left on Miyajima, it is 30 minutes by JR to the five-arch wooden bridge in Iwakuni, Yamaguchi Prefecture. Especially nice in cherry blossom and autumn leaf seasons.
bplan/6/desc: An old port town south of Fukuyama, best combined with Onomichi by rental car. It has a stone lighthouse and alleys known as an anime setting.
bplan/7/title: Walk Around the Hiroshima Castle Moat
bplan/7/desc: Even after the main keep closed, walking the moat and Ninomaru is free. Combined with Shukkeien it takes about an hour, so stop by when you have time left.
nearby_alternatives/0/reason: 40 minutes away by Shinkansen. Kurashiki's Bikan Historical Quarter and Korakuen Garden offer an 'old streets plus garden' combination similar to Miyajima and Onomichi
nearby_alternatives/1/reason: 70 minutes by high-speed boat from Hiroshima Port. For when you want more hot springs, with Dogo Onsen and Matsuyama Castle
nearby_alternatives/2/reason: Far more direct flights and 1 hour by Shinkansen. If you want more food and shopping, stay in Fukuoka and make Hiroshima a day trip
checks/0: Check the Miyajima high and low tide timetable (on the Itsukushima Shrine website) for your travel dates
checks/1: The ¥100 Miyajima visitor tax is added to the ferry fare (since October 2023)
checks/2: The Hiroshima Castle main keep closed on March 22, 2026, and only the exterior can be seen
checks/3: The Yamato Museum reopened after renovation in April 2026, with admission of ¥1,000 and closed on Tuesdays
checks/4: A single IC card (Suica, ICOCA or PASMO) works on most JR lines, streetcars and ferries
checks/5: From April 2026, a Hiroshima Prefecture accommodation tax (around ¥200 per person per night) is added to lodging costs (to be confirmed)
checks/6: Around August 6, lodging rates rise because of the Peace Memorial Ceremony and the area around the park is restricted
checks/7: Oysters are in season from October to March. Farmed oysters are available in summer too, but avoid raw oysters
checks/8: Deer eat paper and plastic, so on Miyajima keep maps and receipts in your bag
checks/9: Some long-established restaurants still take cash only, so prepare ¥10,000 to ¥20,000 in cash
highlights/1: 50 min from the airport to the city
highlights/4: A red torii gate on the sea
